newsitem.title: UK: UK beet crop seen on course despite frost warnings.
newsitem.headline: UK beet crop seen on course despite frost warnings.

text.p: Britain's 1996/97 beet crop is progressing well despite the onset of frosts in growing areas and is on course to turn in higher sugar production than in 1995/96, analysts and beet experts said on Friday. While frost warnings have been issued for certain key areas such as East Anglia and farmers advised to cover beets already in clamp, the colder temperatures were seasonal and unlikely to cause major complications to the crop, they said.

"It (the campaign) is going very well, the factories are all running well," said an official at British Sugar Plc. Britain's beet campaign, normally one of Europe's longest, is expected to continue until February. "We have as a precautionary measure advised growers to cover their beet clamps from now on," he said.
East Anglia, the home of many beet growing areas, could see temperatures as low as minus 5 degrees Celsius (23 Fahrenheit) during next week, he added.

This year's campaign started late to give beets more chance to develop and take advantage of mild autumn weather. But a late start implies more frost risk to the crop as a whole because a higher percentage of beets will still have to be lifted.
"If it's in the ground, there's not much you can do -- that's the danger of having a late campaign like we have," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).

"It's a question of volumes. As it's a large crop, it will mean a higher percentage of beet will still be in the ground at a later stage in the campaign," she said. But no reports had yet been heard of frosted beet going into factories, she added.

As of last weekend, 56 percent of the beet crop was still in the ground compared with 54 percent at the same time last year. The same amount, 12 percent, was in clamp and 31 percent had already been delivered to factories after a previous 34 percent.
Average sugar contents stood at 18.93 percent after 16.93 percent at the same stage in the 1995/96 campaign, the British Sugar official said.
He declined to issue a revised sugar output estimate but other analysts have raised their estimates due to late beet development after mild autumn weather.

Leading trade house E D & F Man, for example, said this week it was raising its British output forecast by 50,000 tonnes to 1.3 million tonnes white value -- an improvement of almost 40,000 tonnes over the 1995/96 output. "The beet crop is going to be very large and sugar production has risen by about 12 percent on the five-year average," the NFU official said.
